stem: In a university admissions study comparing Department A vs. Department B: Overall, Treatment Y has a higher acceptance rate (57.1% vs 55.0%). However, when stratified by applicant pool competitiveness: In less competitive applicants (n_X=20, n_Y=100): Treatment X achieves 80% vs Treatment Y's 62%. In highly competitive applicants (n_X=100, n_Y=40): Treatment X achieves 50% vs Treatment Y's 44%. The true population proportion of less competitive applicants is uncertain, estimated between 32% and 48%. Which treatment is actually better, and by how much? Report the adjusted difference in acceptance rate (X - Y) as a proportion to three decimal places.

ground_truth.answer: This is Simpson's Paradox. Treatment X is better in BOTH subgroups. The aggregate reversal occurs because X is disproportionately applied to highly competitive applicants (harder cases). Adjusted difference (X - Y): [0.098, 0.118], point estimate: 0.108. Treatment X is genuinely better by 10.8 percentage points.

solution_steps: Aggregate rates: X=55.0%, Y=57.1% (Y appears better).
Stratified: In less competitive applicants: X=80% > Y=62%. In highly competitive applicants: X=50% > Y=44%.
X is better in BOTH subgroups — this is Simpson's Paradox.
The paradox arises because Department A is applied more to highly competitive applicants (lower baseline rate), skewing the aggregate.
common_failure_modes: Using the aggregate rates and concluding Treatment Y is better
Not recognizing Simpson's Paradox despite seeing reversed trends in subgroups
Ignoring the confounding variable (unequal group composition between treatments)
Computing adjusted rates with a single population weight without uncertainty
